utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please call the case, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic -- is it okay now? This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. This morning, 28 October 2009, I greet the accused, the Counsel, the witness, the representatives of the Prosecution, and all the people who are assisting us. I would like to tell Ms. Alaburic that she still has one hour and seven minutes, and therefore I now yield and give her the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP, to all the Defence teams, to you, Witness, Mr. Gorjanc, and to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, we concluded for the day yesterday by the Presiding Judge asking you about the possibility of passing from East Mostar on through Jablanica. I will be abandoning the subject for the time being, as we are about to embark on that particular subject matter in some detail when we start talking about the siege of Mostar. Let us now press on with the subject of Muslim soldiers in the HVO as a security issue. Mr. Gorjanc, I will now be showing you a total of five documents in order to ask you something about the documents eventually. The first document is P1438, 1438, which is a report by the commander of Sector West of the Croatian Army -- or, rather, Sector South. He was surveilling units of -- controlling units of the 1st HVO Brigade. In his report, by way of conclusion towards the very end of the report, second paragraph from the bottom up, he says: "The defence security has been reduced because of a considerable number of Muslims in the unit by over 50 per cent." This document dates back to February 1993. The next document, P2223, 2223, that's right, a security report of the SIS chief in the Ljubuski HVO Brigade. In the lower half of the first page, it says: "Through the brigade command, I proposed for the Muslim soldiers --" or, rather, "Muslim conscripts to be disarmed through sending all of them back after they come back from the front-line." The next document in your binder is one you should skip because we are not allowed to use it. Nevertheless, please look at 4D290, 4D290 -- 49 -- or 4D290 -- 920, 4D920, 9, 920. There. This is an SIS report for the 3rd Brigade of the HVO. It comprises several components that are of interest to us. If we look at page 1, it talks about Hajro Jakirovic who did not return to duty -- or had not returned to duty since the 9th of May, after which an SIS official visited him for the purpose of getting back a Motorola and a vehicle. If you move on to page 2, you see the part where it says "MPD." It reads: "The Muslims left the unit for which reason there wasn't sufficient manpower." Then you have the page which ends in number 6, but it will be quite sufficient for you to focus on what I am saying. It reads that weapons were taken from the Muslim members of the 3rd Brigade who had refused to participate in the defence effort. It goes on to say that all the Croats fled from Blagaj. Nevertheless, there was every indication that there were two different currents within the Muslim component, those who were in favour of the HVO and those who were in favour of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all the other unnecessary microphones be switched off, please. We can't hear counsel properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So much for these two documents, and the next one we're look at is P2562.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just tell the interpreters that only my microphone is on. Nevertheless, my colleague, Mr. Stewart -- okay. I do apologise. I was wrong. The mike has been switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P2562, which is a document of the Command of the 3rd Battalion of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, dated May 1993, it reads -- the first thing I'll mention is the second sentence under paragraph 1: "Of a total of 56 members of Muslim ethnicity, 39 are on their way to the positions occupied by the Chetniks, two are participating in all of the actions, and to the best of our knowledge, none of them have gone over to the BH Army side yet." The last thing that paragraph 2 says: "Regarding the activities of our service, the IPD, since the best part of the Muslims are being sent to the [indiscernible] positions, we are permanently in touch with these men. We are trying to explain to them our positions and the need for a shared life. The Muslims feel protected by us, although not fully. We believe that these persons will remain with our units, but more as a result of actually inhabiting an environment that is predominantly Croat." Another report, 2D1379, 1379. This is a report by the SIS Administration, dated July 1993. The Croatian, towards the end of page 1, says there is a special problem that has been occurring with certain units. There are many non-Croat soldiers involved in these units, for the best part Muslims. The importance of this warning was particularly underlined by a recent attack by the BH Army against the HVO in Bijelo Polje, when Muslim HVO soldiers from the unit crossed over to fight alongside the BH Army and went on to form the most powerful Muslim unit as well as in the attack against Dubravska Plateau and Gubavica. Based on these documents, Mr. Gorjanc, had you been a representative of any of the military authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, would you have believed the Muslim soldiers of the HVO to potentially constitute a security threat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now move on to the next set of documents talking about the activities of the BH Army in relation to Muslim soldiers of the HVO. Most of these documents are exhibits already. Therefore, I'll just go through them very quickly yet again, and then I'll be asking you a question at the very end of this exercise, Mr. Gorjanc. The first document is 4D1461. Mr. Gorjanc, can you look at the document, please? I'll be asking you a special question about this document, because this document has not been made an exhibit, or at least not so far. This is an official note on an interview by the SIS, dated September 1992. Midway through paragraph 3, roughly speaking, it reads: "Based on intelligence received on the 16th of September this year, in the evening hours, Muharem Dizdar, one of the HVO commanders, and Ragib Dizdar visited members of the Muslim HVO, telling them not to leave the HVO units or, rather, not to join the BH Army until the hour struck, and they would be informing them in time." Mr. Gorjanc, would you believe an SIS note like this to be of any relevance, security-wise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you, had you been in a position of military authority receiving a document like this, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly have taken some preemptive measures, some precaution. I would have observed the behaviour of Muslim soldiers. I would possibly have transferred them to another front where their refusal to obey orders or opting out of the fighting itself would not have caused that much damage to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I may misunderstand something, as can happen. I wonder what the weight of these documents now is. Normally, a witness for a document is to say whether it's correct, whether he can see that it's genuine, something of that kind. If that is not possible, it is also possible that the witness says, I know about these facts. Now, this witness doesn't say anything about the document, itself. He doesn't say anything about the facts the document speaks about. You only ask him a hypothetical question, so all we have, actually, is a hypothetical judgement, what would the witness do if he were faced with a certain situation. I wonder whether you want to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be glad to oblige and tell you about this. Mr. Gorjanc is not a fact witness, nor, indeed, did we have any discussions along these lines. That wasn't his task. He can't tell us whether what the document claims is, in fact, true or false. He can't tell us whether it's authentic or not, and that's not what we expect him to do. We expect him to tell us what, based on such facts as we are presenting, he, as a military expert, given his background and knowledge, would have done in a particular situation. I'm eliciting his opinion, in other words. As for all these documents, we shall be discussing these from a factual or fact-driven perspective with other witnesses. What we wanted Mr. Gorjanc to help us with was to discuss all these circumstances and aspects. If everything that the documents claim is true, what would a commander do? And then the next witness will be here to corroborate the truthfulness of such facts as are claimed in these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I consider this a very satisfactory answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have followed what was said about the problem, and I would like you to specify this. As Ms. Alaburic says, you're here as an expert witness who, in a given situation, is going to enlighten the Judges by the knowledge which you have of the problems. I will take another example. When you were in the JNA during the "Cold War," let's imagine that the officers of your regiment would have been in contact with a Western power, and this during the Cold War, and that someone would have come to tell them, Wait for a signal eventually to join the Western power. In such an assumption, such a hypothesis, what would you have done, you, yourself, if you had been commanding this regiment? What would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that eventuality, my duty would have been to report this to the Security Service bodies, no more than that, and also to stop any such suspects from obtaining relevant information and data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you say, with a relatively high degree of precision, what sort of fate an officer or soldier like that would have been facing if the KOS would have started looking into their activities in relation to a third country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We established yesterday that I wasn't, myself, working for the KOS. I'm not fully privy to their working methods. I think they would have continued to monitor this person. They would have interviewed this person. If there was any circumstantial evidence that was found, charges would probably have been pressed. There were, in fact, cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next document now. Just keep listening to me, please, Mr. Gorjanc. This is 4D469, 4D469. The second bullet says: "There is pressure being exerted on the Muslims in the HVO and MUP units. There is pressure being exerted on the Muslims in the HVO and MUP units to leave these units. Should they fail to oblige, they shall be threatened by physical liquidation and their houses being set alight." The next document is a BH Army document, 4D33, 4D33. It's a BH Army document that reads: "Call on all Muslims, members of the HVO, to side with their own people." The next document, 4D34, 4D34. Likewise, a BH Army document which reads, bullet number 3 from the bottom up: "Establish cooperation with our own fighters in the HVO and point out the seriousness of the situation to them." The next document is 4D35, yet another BH Army document. The last section of paragraph 3 reads: "The IPD, the Morale and Religious Issues Department, will set up a plan in relation to, among others, Muslims in HVO units in the municipalities of Capljina and Stolac." The next document, 4D36, again a BH Army document, early May 1993. Item 3, bullet point 2, reads: "We have linked up with our own men in the HVO." It then goes on to say: "Men from the Capljina HVO have been given the task of taking the village of Tasovcici and the bridge in Capljina, the objective being to stop any forces from being brought in from the general Metkovic direction." It then goes on to say: "The taking of the town of Stolac with our own men in the HVO." Next document, 2D288, 288, another BH Army document signed by Fikret Muslimovic. Do you know that person, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I first met Fikret Muslimovic in 1988. He was one of the men very close and deep to -- and deeply trusted by the late BH president, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muslimovic concludes by saying that it was realistic to expect the tensions to keep on mounting with the HVO. In that situation, it was exceptionally important to make the Muslims in the HVO as passive as possible and try to get them to leave the ranks of the HVO and join, instead, the BH Army. Mr. Gorjanc, knowing, as you do, the author of this document, would you attach any sort of importance to this document at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exceptional importance, as a matter of fact, since he was the chief of the Military Security and Intelligence Service of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, 4D473. Towards the end of paragraph 2, it reads -- and the author of this document is a commander, the commander of a unit of the BH Army. This was dispatched in writing to the commander of the 1st HVO Brigade. The BH Army commander says: "I would like to mention, and this is very well known to you, that a large number of Muslims -- Muslim soldiers are in your formations. They are ethnic Muslims and belong to this people. Therefore, it would not be good if a certain defined organisation and formation of your units were to be disrupted." How would you interpret this sentence, Mr. Gorjanc? What would your interpretation have been had you received this, had this been sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a threat that he would be withdrawing his own fellow ethnic Muslims from these units, and if that were, would have seriously threatened the combat readiness of my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Because we don't have much time, unfortunately, I will be skipping the next three documents covering the same subject, and I will try to ask you a question by way of conclusion. Mr. Gorjanc, had you been forewarned by your own Security Service or the SIS about Muslim soldiers constituting a potential threat, had you known that these warnings were based on such documents of the BH Army as we have seen or mentioned, had you known something else, probably from other sources, something that wasn't in writing, would you have considered these Muslims to constitute a security threat or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, let us posit this security threat and let's say it actually happened. You were an HVO commander losing control over a significant portion of your own territory simply because you were betrayed by soldiers of another ethnicity from within your own ranks. What sort of reaction would you have put in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have considered that to be an act of treason, and I would have taken any steps available to me, including the pressing of charges against those deserters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what would you have done about the Muslim soldiers remaining in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a situation that called for determined and urgent action, I would probably have disarmed and isolated those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, two questions very similar to these the military expert for the Prosecution, Mr. Pringle, answered, which was recorded on page 24265, his answers were positive when asked whether a military commander would have considered Muslims a military threat. He said, Yes, I think so. Can we then conclude that you agree with the OTP expert on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the third binder I'm going to skip the topic of the military significance of Central Bosnia because I would like to dedicate more time to the siege of Mostar. Therefore, the following topic is the siege of Mostar and whether it existed or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, for this section you received certain materials from the Defence, and you were requested to provide your opinion and say whether the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we speak about the siege of Mostar, Witness, in the sequence of questions you just had, I wish to ask you one question. We have for the last four years a great number of elements coming both from Prosecution and Defence, and with these elements we note that there had been units of the HVO which were constituted with important numbers of Muslim soldiers, sometimes units where the majority of soldiers were Muslims, so we have to keep this in mind. Also, at the time corresponding to these documents we know that there were negotiations in Geneva in progress where apparently there appeared to be constitution of a single army, constituted both of soldiers of the HVO and of Muslim soldiers, possibly even at the time of the absorptions of one group by the other one under either Croatian command or Bosnian command. So all this at the time seemed to be very much in everybody's mind. A brigade commander in such a situation, which is very complex on the political plane and also complex on the military plane, because then these soldiers, while there was a conflict in progress, could have certain consequences. Now, you are an expert witness. In a situation which is so complex, what were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that a brigade commander did not know all the facts with regard to the negotiations in Geneva, and he acted based on concrete situations as they evolved in his area of responsibility. And I would have acted in the same context, and I would have undertaken the measures that I've already mentioned. I would be cautious. I would put soldiers of a different ethnicity under surveillance. I would have moved them to an area where they would not have posed a threat to my state, and ultimately I would isolate them and disarm them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to finish by completing my question. We know that in the several armies at the time, whether the Serbian or Bosniak or Croatian, there was, in the military apparatus, different ethnical groups, officers who belonged to another ethnical group. As an example, in the BiH you had Colonel Merdan who was a Croatian, and I could quote a certain number of examples. In such a situation, or at the higher level, higher echelon, in the responsibility role of the officers of a different or another ethnic group, and on the -- in the field, on the ground, there are also soldiers of another ethnic group, the brigade commander, did he have -- with all these elements, do what you have just said? And what I have added to my question, does it change your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, those were individuals. They could not have a significant impact on the situation in the area of responsibility and on the front-line. Secondly, those individuals were mostly in high positions for political reasons. This was to show to the general public that in the ranks of the army or any other military - it doesn't really matter - there were also soldiers of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your answer. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. For a few minutes, we are going to have some people from the United Nations -- officials from the United Nations who have to come and sit with the Registrar. Usher, please, could you bring in the people who will be present during the hearing -- who will attend the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll have the witness escorted outside the courtroom, because he needs to meet with a representative of the Witness and Victim Unit, who has got to give him something. We'll wait a few minutes. Usher, please escort the witness outside the courtroom. He'll be back in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, could you please check with the witness, whether Mr. Merdan was indeed a Croat? Mr. Merdan's name is -- name is Dzemal. I believe they know each other from the Yugoslav People's Army. Maybe you should ask him who that person Merdan was. He was in a prominent position in the 3rd Corps, as you have said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier on I asked a question which, in my view, was clear, but it seems that there is a need to have you specify. Did you know Colonel Merdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've never been stationed with him or served with him within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And in your report, which you drafted on the basis of the documents, have you noticed that there was a Dzemal Merdan who once -- who held a high position within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I did come across that name when I was dealing with Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You've seen the name, but you've never served with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this Dzemal Merdan, was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, judging by the name, he is a Muslim, Dzemal or Dzemo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, based on the document that we have just seen, would you say that the BiH Army fostered cooperation with the HVO or maybe it tried to create a different atmosphere with regard to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the documents that were available to me, the BiH Army, throughout that entire time, had its own agenda and its own views to the engagement of Muslims in the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the topic of the siege of Mostar. Just a remark, Mr. Gorjanc, and I hope my learned friends from the OTP will not object to my next leading question. Tell me, was your task to provide an opinion as to whether it may be said about the East of Mostar to be under siege or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the question put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the document, and then we will arrive at a conclusion. First of all, let's look at the territory around East Mostar which was under the control of the Muslim authorities after the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one remark for the Trial Chamber. We will be dealing with the period after the 30th of June, 1993, because before that date the BiH Army had communication with its units in Jablanica. Having said that, I would like to say that it had to go through the territory that was under the control of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's first look at 4D625. This is a map -- 4D625 is a map of the territory of East Mostar in mid-July 1993. Here we can see an area from East Mostar southwards and northward. From East Mostar to Jablanica, how far is that? What's the distance; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in the direction of Blagaj and Buna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that the Praljak Defence also showed a map of that situation. IC1005 and IC1006 are the numbers of the maps presented by the Praljak Defence. And now I'm going to talk about documents that speak about communication between Jablanica and East Mostar. I'm going to go through the documents, as fast as I can, and then we will arrive at a conclusion about that communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first document is 2D1389. And in that document, in a section dealing with the zone of responsibility of the 4th Corps, it is stated what area north of East Mostar was conquered by the BH Army, and in conclusion it is stated that the 4th and the 6th Corps linked up. One question, Mr. Gorjanc. Do you perhaps know where was the headquarters of the 4th Corps and where was the headquarters of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Corps was headquartered in Mostar, whereas the command post of the 6th Corps was in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What would you say about the linking up of the two corps, from the point of view of communication between Jablanica and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the operative zone of the 6th and the 4th Corps were joined and they had an unhindered communication between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D768 is the following document, 4D768, a document issued by Rasim Delic. Under item 3, there is a reference to transport between Igman and Mostar. Mr. Gorjanc, from the point of view of communication of Mostar north of -- north of Mostar, towards Jablanica, was that possible or not, judging by this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this document, communication was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is under seal, so I would kindly ask the Registrar not to broadcast it. And the document number is P3858. It is an UNPROFOR information. It says -- Sulejman Budakovic, the commander of the BiH Army, says that the Presidency will agree to the cease-fire, but that they had to keep corridors in the direction of Jablanica. What would you conclude, based on this document? Was there communication between Mostar and Jablanica, was it possible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they wanted to maintain it, then that means that they actually had it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is also under seal, P4447, and this document under item 1, midway, it says that the Muslim refugees from Capljina arrived in Mostar on the east bank of the Neretva and that they were headed towards Jablanica. Tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, does this confirm or deny the possibility of communication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document confirms it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D780 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. This document which is before us, Mr. Expert Witness, shows that the Capljina refugees arrived in Mostar. Now, if the refugees travel and arrive in Mostar, this means that the HVO didn't prevent them from passing through, because they must have travelled on roads controlled by the ABiH; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is what refugees we're talking about; are they from the right bank of the River Neretva or, rather, from the left bank? On the left bank, there were no obstacles on the part of the HVO. The HVO could not have prevented their arrival. As for the right bank, they should have crossed one of the bridges, either in Capljina or in Zitomislic. That means that the HVO did not prevent their arrival in any way, irrespective of the banks that they came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, no translation. You are going a bit too fast, Ms. Alaburic. It's hardly possible to follow you. When we have the document, you say three words, the witness says, Yes, or, No, or nothing, and you switch to the next, and we are trying to run breathless behind you. I'm sorry, maybe it's because we are old, but please have some regards to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will show every form of consideration. I'm not young myself. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question was this: If I understood your answer to Judge Antonetti's question properly, if the refugees arrived in East Mostar along the left bank, then they were moving through the territory that was not under the control of the Croatian authorities or the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The following document is 4D780. I'm going to repeat my question. Mr. Gorjanc, my question has not been properly recorded so I'll repeat it. We are not talking about soldiers, but rather refugees. If refugees were arriving at East Mostar from the south, along the left bank, were they supposed to cross the territory that was under the control of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the counsel said "southern bank." I suppose that she meant "eastern bank." In that case, the HVO could not have prevented them from doing so unless they used an infantry fire, and judging by the document, there was no infantry fire opened at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And as for the physical control over the territory, who exerted territory [as interpreted] over that territory, who exerted control?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army exerted control over that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll start skipping documents gradually, simply because we're running out of time and we have no time to go through all of these documents. Mr. Gorjanc, you've seen them all. Let's look at 3D939, 3D939. This document talks about the involvement of a brigade of the BH Army along the following axis: Vrdi-Goranci, and then on towards Mostar. Is this to the south of East Mostar or in a different direction, or, rather, is this to the north?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is to the north, the western Neretva River bank. This is the only viable route from the Dreznica river valley directly through on to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now 3D932. Paragraph 2 reads: "The area of the 4th Corps of the BH Army is the place that, based on an agreement, one or two companies must be sent to, following an agreement from the composition of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the 3rd BH Army Corps." Can you tell us more about this? What would this mean? How come that all of a sudden a unit is arriving in the Mostar area from the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HQ of the 7th Muslim Brigade was in Zenica, Central Bosnia. It was the manoeuvring unit of the 3rd Corps. I say "manoeuvring unit" or a "manoeuvre unit" in the meaning we explained yesterday used to conduct operations throughout the territory of the 3rd Corps, which means that it was now on its way there in order to strengthen -- reinforce the 4th Corps in its operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The unit from Central Bosnia was now about to arrive in the Mostar area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next document, 4D719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is an important topic. So we have this document 3D00932. This is a document from the 4th Corps, signed Pasalic, which establishes that the 7th Brigade or a few companies of that brigade which were subordinated to the 3rd Corps, as everyone knows, will go to the area under the control of the 4th Corps. And everyone knows that the 4th Corps is Mostar. As far as you're concerned, and I'm talking from a military point of view, does this document show that the units of the BiH from Zenica could go and reach Mostar without any problem whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how many problems there were in that specific situation, in actual fact, but, yes, it would have been able to arrive there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In this light, would you agree, as a military expert, with the fact that one can say that Mostar is a city under siege, like Sarajevo, or that Mostar is in a different kind of situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostar was in a substantially different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the north, where the main reserves of the BH Army were, there were two roads leading. One was down the Neretva River Valley, which was most probably under fire, under artillery fire, HVO artillery fire. The other route took one across a mountainous area, the western slopes of Mount Prenj and on towards Jablanica. That route was not under fire by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that the situation in Mostar was different from the situation in Sarajevo, do you say so because you're familiar with the situation of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, to quite a considerable degree I have emotional links to Sarajevo, myself, and I closely followed everything that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have more questions on this document and the conclusions it allows to take. What would you say -- what kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an information document. The 4th Corps Command informs the forward command post of the Supreme Command Staff in Jablanica of something that's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then why is it called "Order"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see the word "Order" anywhere. It would be impossible for the 4th Corps to exercise command over a part of the Supreme Command itself which at this point in time happens to be at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There must be, then, a problem in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, we're not seeing the word "Order." If Your Honour could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe I have it wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- draw to our attention where, because at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I think I'm probably on the wrong document. I'm awfully sorry. I was on the previous document, which was an order, and in -- okay, thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To err is human. We are entirely sympathetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, do you know whether a single unit of the BH Army could, in fact, enter Sarajevo while Sarajevo was under siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for a fact that any unit actually went in, but I know that there was a unit that came out. Several units reached Igman, as well as Cemerno, Vares as well, and Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. 4D -- 4D719. Mr. Gorjanc, try to focus on what I'm about to read out to you. I will be quoting several portions of this document from October 1993. This is a 4th Corps document of the BH Army. The second paragraph down towards the very end reads: "It was established that it is necessary to stop all traffic on the main road while relieving personnel at positions held by this company, due to an increased activity by the enemy and action taken against men and vehicles." Mr. Gorjanc, does this not mean that the BH Army units were, as a rule, moving down this main road?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At this point I'm going to object to the question. Again, I understand Ms. Alaburic is trying to get through these documents, but the last question was so clearly leading, I feel I have to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, yesterday I cautioned you to be careful and to work on a step-by-step basis by first submitting the document to the witness, saying, This is what this paragraph says, this is the second document, then ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I entirely agree with my learned friend. I do apologise for my leading question. But there is this sentence that seems so self-explanatory, but I'm slightly uncomfortable about it, and therefore I'll have to ask an open-ended question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The sentence that we've just read out, Mr. Gorjanc, what follows from that? What was the axis along which the BH units were deploying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the company was in the immediate vicinity of the Mostar-Jablanica main road. It was most probably for that reason that problems were occurring. As people were travelling down that road, it was more difficult to take shifts because the HVO could at any point in time open fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about this claim that the document makes? This is page 3 of the Croatian, and we'll give you an English reference as well: "A large problem for the command of the operations group was presented by the transport of civilian population and everyone else marching north and south." My question, Mr. Gorjanc: If you think back to that map that we looked at at the beginning of this examination, or, rather, as we first started discussing this subject, how would you explain this, the expansion of civilian population to the north and south?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were probably moving down a mountain road and across the western slopes of Mount Prenj. The road must have been broad enough for them to be able to advance in both directions, north and south, with no hindrance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the towns towards which they were moving, if they were heading north and south?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: North would have meant Jablanica and then on to Konjic, and on to Sarajevo from there across Mount Igman. You couldn't actually access the city of Sarajevo, itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about south?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have meant Mostar. Across Jablanica and then on to Mostar, and onwards to Buna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you head south of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Buna and Blagaj, and then down towards the coast, as everyone knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "There are enormous problems being faced with the transport of the wounded and everything else for the city. There is a need that is underlying to repair an APC to be used for these purposes during night-time." Mr. Gorjanc, if you look at this sentence, what does it lead you to conclude? Were the wounded eventually taken through to Mostar or not? What sort of assistance were they given?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This makes it perfectly clear that they were being taken to Mostar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next sentence: "There was a large problem in terms of supplying bread to this unit because the wood needed for the production of the Mostar Bakery had to be taken to Mostar and then on to Bijelo Polje." Mr. Gorjanc, was there any road connecting Mostar and Bijelo Polje at this point in time or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there certainly was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As we read on, we see something that they refer to as the Cargo Platoon. Mr. Gorjanc, what exactly does that term suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cargo Platoon, as a matter of principle, would comprise 20 or 30 horses used to transport cargo on their backs across mountainous areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, there is talk here of oil being transported dripping down on these horses' backs, opening wounds on the animals, themselves, thus side-lining the animals and putting them out of action. Based on this sentence, what exactly did the BH Army do to bring oil into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were obviously using horses for that purpose. They brought oil in on horseback.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next thing it says is about the fighters along the front-line protesting on a massive scale, among other things, because of the unmasked departure for the north by the civilians and soldiers alike. Mr. Gorjanc, based on this sentence and everything else that we have been talking about, what would you say about the possibility of using the roads from East Mostar, leading towards Jablanica and down further south, Buna and Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to use these roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll be skipping the next two documents. The next one up is 4D798, 798. It's a document by Sefer Halilovic that he dispatched to Rasim Delic in September 1993. If you look at bullet point number 2, we see mention there of a helicopter that was sent into the area to transport the seriously wounded as well as an entire company to the Bijelo Polje sector, only to eventually reach Mostar, itself. Mr. Gorjanc, based on this claim, what could we possibly conclude about whether it was possible to travel back and forth between Jablanica and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was by air, by helicopter, and obviously there were no restrictions on that, in terms of what the army could do. The HVO could have exerted no influence at all over where and whether the helicopters were flying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, also under seal, P9851. The conclusion contained in paragraph 2 of this document reads: "It seems that as of mid-August, there was limited movement by the population between the larger east bank and Jablanica in central Bosnia (to the north and south)." Further down: "A mountain path is used for this purpose, and we are looking at people who are trying to be reunited with their families. Movement is still limited on account of the danger being faced by those travelling along that route and also because of the fact that in order to leave, one must first obtain a permit from the BH Army, which allegedly is very difficult to obtain." We'll be looking at another document now that talks about more or less the same subject, and then we'll be commenting on both documents jointly. I'll be skipping the next document and be calling 4D4545 -- or, rather, 4D545, 545. This is an excerpt from Esad Sejtanic's book. He says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could counsel please provide a reference as to where she's reading from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the interpreters because I'm tuned into the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll just say a single sentence: "Again, a large number of citizens wanted to leave for Jablanica and further into Bosnia. Repressive measures, regrettably, had to be taken to stop the population from leaving on a large scale, and we restricted movement to the extent possible." That was the only passage that was translated into English, and that's why I didn't need to go into more detail. Mr. Gorjanc, at this point in time I would like to know more these observations to the effect that the BH Army were trying to stop the departure of civilian population from Mostar on to Jablanica. Can you explain how such a thing would have been possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there must be a little problem of translation, because the text that we have in the transcript does not correspond exactly to the text in -- on the paper. On the paper, I read: "By repressive measures, regrettably, we prevented the outflow of population and reduced any movement of population to minimum." You, however, have read: "Regrettably, we had -- measures had to be taken," and that's not the same thing, because in the written text here, without any comment, he says: "We took, regrettably, these measures," but what you read means: "We were forced to take these measures," and if that is the correct translation, it would, of course, be interesting to know whether the book anywhere gives an explanation why this was considered necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, obviously what I read out in Bosnian was obviously misinterpreted into English. The accurate translation is what you have in front of you. So this makes no mention of anybody being forced to do anything. The last sentence reads, I quote: "By repressive measures, regrettably, we prevented the outflow of population and reduced any movement of population to a minimum."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, could you please explain to us the situation in which the ABiH is preventing --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. If we can just back up for a moment. I understand previously the question from Ms. Alaburic was: "At this point in time, I would like to go into the observations that the BH Army were trying to stop the departure of the civilian population from Mostar to Jablanica, and can you explain how such a thing would have been possible?" I interrupt now because I object to the question. Mr. Gorjanc, as we know and as has been explained, is not a factual witness, so clearly we cannot be looking for a factual answer. Secondly, in regard to his expertise, this seems to me to be more of a strategic question -- a strategic question, looking for a strategic answer, and I'm not sure that Mr. Gorjanc has the wherewithal to answer such a question where he wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am grateful to my learned friend. I will rephrase my question, but I consider my question to be of a strategic nature, also, and it is a theoretical question. I asked the question under the assumption that what the document says is true, and I want the expert to explain to us how it is possible for the ABiH to prevent the civilian population from leaving Eastern Mostar toward -- northward or southward, which is -- which makes no difference at this point in time. But we consider the question strategic because it is possible for someone to use their own civilian population to attain some objectives, which can be part of a military doctrine or part of a certain practice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, under the assumption that the ABiH, indeed, was preventing the departure of civilian population from Eastern Mostar, can you explain to us, from the point of view of military doctrine and/or practice known to you, how that is possible, if we're speaking about a town which is badly supplied, which is being targeted by enemy artillery, and which the population lives badly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any town defending itself, and where there is population at the same time, the morale of the defenders is much better when they know that they are defending their own people. And in that context, two or three documents back, when soldiers of the ABiH dislike the population leaving northward, this measure was probably taken to raise the morale of the soldiers of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is this a legitimate and legal way of using civilian population, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but the principle is: When a town is being defended, parts of the population, such as women, children and elderly people, are taken out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one more document in this context. This is also under seal. It is P3547, 3547. In paragraph 6, referring to Mostar, under item 2, we can see: "The UNHCR Metkovic have cancelled all aid convoys because the HVO insist on being informed of the percentages of aid being delivered to each side of the population," as written here. If anyone were to say to you that in a certain period, to which this report refers, there were no convoys of humanitarian aid in the area of Mostar, what would you consider to be the cause?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the language used here, I can conclude that the UNHCR cancelled these convoys and that they were unwilling to supply Mostar because the HVO had demanded data on the shares of the aid being dealt out to either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just an intermediate question. Witness, do you know or not whether it is legitimate to put such a condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot say that I know for certain, but it would be logical for those goods, if it passes through territory under the control of the HVO, for them to ask for equal shares to be given to either side because both suffer from shortages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I was only asking about the legal situation, not on what you think is logical. So the answer is, I don't know, as I read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, all the documents which Ms. Alaburic showed you in this last half hour, I checked that all these documents have references in your report. So you've seen these documents, and they enabled you to have your own conclusions, and this is important to have this on the transcript. In the document we now have on the screen, it seems that the HCR cancelled some convoys, and the reason, officially, would be that they wanted to be informed of the percentage of aid which had to be delivered to the populations, in the plural, the people; that is to say, the Croats, the Muslims, possibly the Serbs, because there still were a few left in Mostar. When you saw this, how did you analyse this, in military terms? And this is a follow-up to the question of my colleague. From a military point of view, can a military authority stop a convoy and demand to be told to whom the food is destined? Can -- a military may ask such a question? Because the real cause is that the HVO wanted to know what was -- to whom the humanitarian aid was going, the distribution of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that an army doesn't have the right to raise this issue. But in that context, the HVO was the authority in Herceg-Bosna, and those civilian authorities really closely cooperated with the UNHCR. This is how I read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, a related question. You have explained to us that the axis to East Mostar by road was free. Why do we have here a document where the UNHCR gives clearly the impression that they need approval of the HVO to go to Mostar East? I think that -- it seems to me there is a little contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I spoke about free travel, I was referring to the stretch of road between Buna and Jablanica and not between Buna and Metkovic. That area, up to the border at Doljani, was under the control of HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait. Witness, I'd like things to be quite clear, because all this is very complex and somebody from the outside could really have problems understanding. What you have just said is if the HVO gives its authorisation, it is because it controls a part of the road which it actually controls. But as from a given moment, it becomes the BiH who then controls the road. Is that what you've just told us? Because I'm trying to understand what you've said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. One question seems to be leading to the next here, and the next is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow, I would just like to put a map on the ELMO for you to be able to see how Mostar can be reached from Croatia, because Metkovic is in Croatia, and how you can travel from Mostar to Jablanica, and I believe we will all be more comfortable then. I prepared different types of maps. I'll give you the simplest one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to state that I did not challenge and do not plan to challenge the answer given to me on this subject by the witness. Please give me a sign when you think that I can ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we can see it on the ELMO and if we can discern -- is the map on the ELMO? Oh, here it is now. I believe you will be able to see sufficiently well and that the witness will be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the French interpretation, I didn't get the translation of Ms. Alaburic. Somebody must have forgotten to press the button. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have the map here, where we see the main roads around Mostar. We can see how Mostar can be reached from the south, that is, from the direction of Croatia. To the right is the main road leading to Mostar from Nevesinje, that is, from the territory controlled by the Serbs. And to the north, there is the main road through Bijelo Polje towards Jablanica. I believe that will help us understand what the witness is saying to us better. As far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the HVO controlled an area. What does -- who was that, the HVO who? The operation zone, or the military police, or what does it mean, specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot provide an accurate answer about that unit. That zone was under the responsibility of the south-eastern zone of operations of the HVO, I think, but the relevant documents were not available to me. But I can show you on the map which communication was controlled by the HVO and which by the ABiH, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So the zone controls a certain area, a certain "superficie" of the terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I intervene because this is important. We have the map on the ELMO. Could you, with a pencil, show where the humanitarian convoys start from, where they go through, by which control of the HVO they have to pass? Can you do this quickly just now on the screen so that we see there is no interpretation mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no pen at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, please, could you give the magic pencil to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hereabouts [marks] is Metkovic, and somewhere here [marks] is the border between Bosnia and Croatia. Here [marks] is Buna, and from here [marks] all the way through here [marks], the area was controlled by the ABiH, and this area [indicates] is controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please give an IC number to this map. This map is very important. Right. Madam Registrar, could you please give a number to this map?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be IC1087.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's one minute left until the break. Maybe just one more explanation, to avoid misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, it's about one answer you provided to the question asked by Judge Trechsel. Does the zone of operations have control over a part of territory? If you know, tell us. How was the territory of Herceg-Bosna divided, militarily?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Militarily, it was divided into several zones of operation, one of them being the south-eastern zone, which included the southern and the eastern part of Herzegovina. Another was the north-western part, which included the north of Herzegovina and the west. Then there was the Zone of Operation Central Bosnia in Central Bosnia, and the Zone of Operation Posavina, and the northern part toward the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, when we say "Zone of Operation South-Eastern Herzegovina," is that then simply part of the area of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If, in the area of a zone of operation, there are contact points with the enemy and combat action, and in another part there is no combat, can you tell us where the military is and what it does?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military, in principle, has part of its forces at the front-line and at contact points with the enemy along a stretch that's three to five kilometres wide, and the other units are -- either rest or train or engage in some other non-military activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gorjanc. I believe, Your Honours, that we can now break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to now take the break, and you have about 20 minutes left to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the 20 minutes that we have left, by your leave, would be distributed in the following way: I'll take 13 [Realtime transcript read in error "30"] minutes and General Praljak will take 7 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, given the importance of the topic of communication, I would like to show you another document from the set of documents, 4D780. Maybe you can focus on what I'm going to tell you. This is an order issued by Stjepan Siber. He was the deputy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to correct the transcript because the mathematics are not very convincing. Out of your 20 minutes, you want to take 30, yourself, and you said "13," I'm sure. Not "30 minutes," "13." That's just a correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did say "13," and I'm sorry that you were the one who spotted this mistake. If you hadn't spotted the mistake, maybe I would have ended up having 30 minutes, instead of 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the document. You have it on the screen, Mr. Gorjanc. Let's see what the deputy commander of the BiH Army says in the document: "The main goal of the aggressors, the HVO and the HV," as he defines them, "is to cut off communication between Prozor and Jablanica and thus block the Mostar-Jablanica-Sarajevo axis." Mr. Gorjanc, please tell us, based on this document, what can you tell us about communication across Jablanica from Mostar to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this document, that communication was free to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to ask you whether the civilian population could also use it, but we will deal with that later. In paragraph 215 of your report, you provide your conclusions about the topic of the siege of Mostar and whether it actually existed or not, based on the documents that you had available to you. Could you please share with us your conclusion? Did the siege of Mostar exist or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the thorough study of all the documents that were available to me and based on the military theory, I can conclude that Mostar, as a city, was never besieged in the classical way. It was never closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gorjanc, a few very brief questions about the eighth paragraph of your report, which is the military significance of Central Bosnia/North Herzegovina. You attached a number of maps with your report. Could you please tell us who is the author of the maps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted them, personally, in the CorelDRAW programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to list the documents which are maps. 4D1486, 4D1485, 4D1484, 4D1491, and 4D1483. In paragraph 201 of your report, you, Mr. Gorjanc, provide a conclusion as to why, from a military aspect, it would be desirable for an army in the area to conquer and place under its control the territory of Konjic. Could you tell us, briefly, why is Konjic so important?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I please be shown the record on the screen because I have an e-court document on both screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please oblige. Mr. Gorjanc has been very disciplined and has been following the record or the transcript of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The military significance of Konjic, can you tell us a sentence or two?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konjic is midway between Sarajevo and Mostar. From Konjic -- or, rather, the general territory of Konjic and Jablanica is the departure point of three roads, from Makljen to Bugojno, from Kiseljak, Dusina to Neretvica, and the third main road from Mostar across [indiscernible] in the direction of Konjic and onwards to Mostar. At the same time, from Mostar you could launch military operations in the direction of more towards Igman, with a view to lifting the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you said "from Mostar across Igman"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. From Konjic across Mount Igman towards Sarajevo, from Konjic along the right bank or, rather, in the middle part of the flow of the Neretva towards Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, and finally from Konjic in the direction of Mostar. Moreover, in Konjic was the factory of ammunition called Igman, ranging from calibre 4.5 to 14.5 millimetres. The former states of the former Yugoslavia were supplied from there, and it also manufactured for the BiH Army. In Konjic, there was also a large and significant facility of the military command, the ARK facility, the Atomic War Command that belonged to the army. Under the conditions of a nuclear war, this would have been the headquarters of the military command of the former state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gorjanc. What about Vitez and its significance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vitez was extremely important as a factory of explosives. That was the largest and perhaps the only factory of explosives in the former state, and it also produced gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now what about Bugojno, Travnik, and Novi Travnik; what made them significant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bugojno had a factory, known as Slavko Rodic, which manufactured mines, ammunition for light anti-artillery weapons, and ignition devices for various types of ammunition. In Travnik, there was a manufacturing plant for military gear, and there was an overhaul institute for the electrical devices such as radios and the like. And in Novi Travnik, there was the biggest factory of heavy artillery that ever was in the former state, which produced cannons, artillery guns, multi-rocket-launchers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, when we are talking about communication along the Neretva Valley down to the Adriatic coast, why is that important?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the basic communication of the former state from north to south, from Posavina down to the Adriatic coast.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I'm going to have a few very brief questions about the rest of your expert report. In Chapter 11, you're dealing with "asanacija," the clearing up of the terrain. I'm going to ask you to provide your explanation about the clearing up of the terrain from the remains of the enemy army. This is translated as a clear-up operation or a mop-up operation, and in B/C/S it's "asanacija." Mr. Gorjanc, when it comes to such operations, the clearing up of the terrain, can they be considered ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Chapter 12, Mr. Gorjanc, you are analysing the topic of re-subordination. Is there such a thing as automatic re-subordination?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Any re-subordination had to be preceded by a decision and an order of the superior to both units, the unit that is being re-subordinated and the unit to which that first one is re-subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the next chapter, you analyse the term "staff tasks," and in paragraph 258 you say that in every military, the General Staff does not have the authority of direct command over operative and strategic or only operative troops, but when it comes to minor tasks, the Supreme Command can transfer its responsibilities to the General Staff. If I remember General Praljak's testimony well, he formulated his understanding of his own authorities in almost an identical way. Could you please establish a link between the staff functions of the General Staff with the possibility for the General Staff to have command responsibilities under certain conditions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That command responsibility of the General Staff can apply to the system of training of units, commands and staffs, to the internal organisation of certain units, or, rather, to the instructions for issuing decisions, assessing situations, monitoring a situation on the battle-field, and so on and so forth. It doesn't have anything to do with commanding units as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, finally, concluding provisions and issues, Mr. Gorjanc, if troops are isolated, arrested, or placed in custody, if one's own troops are isolated, does an incarcerated soldier lose the status of a soldier in such an army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, a hypothetical situation for you to consider. If you had been a member of the military authorities in Herceg-Bosna, and if you had planned a conflict with the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in view of your understanding and knowledge of the peoples of the former Yugoslavia, the circumstances, customs, and the history, would you have created the HVO as an army with a huge percentage of Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would certainly have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my last question, again a hypothetical one. If, in the early 1990s, you had been the president of the Republic of Croatia, and if you had planned to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if you had planned to annex part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia, knowing fully well that that would mean a conflict with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so you obviously would have had to plan for such a conflict, would you have armed the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you have assisted in the training of its soldiers and officers, would you have helped the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that had been my intention, I certainly would not have done all those things. I would not have assisted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Gorjanc. Thank you for your cooperation and your answers. Your Honours, this brings my examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have seven minutes for military issues. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gorjanc.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: A question was asked about something earlier on, how much time does it take to establish an army, something to that effect. My question is: Can one establish an organised army of an organised country, in terms of the degree of civilisation, democracy, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday that the existence of a state is the precondition for the existence of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So if we were, for example, to send Iraqi troops, for example, in Iraq, or to send there, to join the Iraqi troops, 300 American instructors, does that mean that within six months it would turn into an armed force as effective as the US Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your hypothetical example clearly shows that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were an officer of the JNA and you wanted to go abroad someplace, Trieste, for example, did you need to ask for permission to go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The last thing was in 1988, the Division Command was supposed to issue me with a permit to travel abroad. When I did for the very first time back in 1977, I needed approval from Belgrade in order to travel abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Once back, what exactly did you have to write up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I was back, I had to write up a special report, what I saw abroad, in the sense of military relevance, and who I was communicating with while abroad. In the last period, it was no longer necessary to write these reports, except, of course, if we came across anything that we believed was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, in an army like that, or any other army, if it was observed that there was a certain group of soldiers and officers preparing an armed rebellion against their own army, how would you qualify an action like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thirdly, you saw the documents and you concluded that the BH Army was attacking the HVO in the hills; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they were attacking, but what the documents show is that they had the intentions to issue order like that -- to issue orders like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The main road, Mostar-Jablanica-Konjic-Tarcin-Visoko-Zenica, what about that road, based on your investigations of the Central Bosnia subject matter; could that road be used?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the way up to Bilalovac, it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on, thank you. You said the HVO could use its artillery in the Bijelo Polje area in order to control that road. The BH Army was in Dreznica; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about -- what about night-time, night-time? What is the visibility like? Can the artillery target anything at all, or could anyone at all could have used that road during night-time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite know what sort of night-vision equipment the HVO was using, but I think more advanced equipment was only being introduced into the JNA and the range -- the night-vision range would have been up to 2.000 metres, provided visibility was good. That was the -- that was the extreme range, but it really depended on a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Assuming someone was attacking you from the hills, would it have exceeded those two kilometres, if there was rain, for example, or cloud banks, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, one speaker at a time, please, kindly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We didn't get the last answer, and if the gentlemen could pause because we, too, are interested in the answers. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Assuming, and we've seen that all here, that the BH Army was attacking Vrda from the direction of Dreznica, what about the distance of the HVO artillery positions; would it have exceeded the two kilometres within which it was possibly or feasible to observe that road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been more. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Did it make it into the transcript? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
