utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if it's true that the HVO was on one side, along the north-south axis, and the BH Army on the opposite side - let's forget about the VRS for the time being - in any given case, any given eventuality, could one speak of that town being surrounded, given the fact that there was a road leading to Zenica that was open?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And my last question. His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you the following question: Did the HVO zone control a certain area? We don't know what they mean by "area" or by "control." You said any normal army would have kept a third of its men along the front-line facing the enemy, another third where they could put them up, and perhaps another third behind the lines, depending on developments in terms of combat; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this last third would be in their own homes, family homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The HVO -- you looked at those documents. Did you see, do you remember, that a third of its manpower would be taken to the front-line, and that was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, because those documents were not available to me, not in that sense, not from the HVO side. And as far as my personal observations go, this was the actual situation. That would be my personal conclusion, but I've seen no documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's assume that this was the case. You are an expert. The HVO had a third of a brigade mobilised somewhere along the front-line. Would they have any other lines, any people behind the lines, in the rear, as they say, and then after that could you tell me what this army could possibly be controlling, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Registrar tells us that you have used nine minutes, while your time is seven minutes, which means that you're already off limits and you should wrap up. Please finish your question, and then it will be over. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So an army's holding this front-line. What is this army actually controlling, what can it possibly control? And, secondly, what is the real territory under their control? And, thirdly, what do you mean by "control"? That's the last thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, there are three questions. You were told to ask one question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, this has been raised as a problem. Judge Trechsel, as a matter of fact, you did. What are they controlling and what is territory? Let's look into these matters. What is the territory and what is the control? Let's try to define these concepts. What is the territory and what is the control? Yeah, well, right, that is the way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, there may later be opportunities, but you had a certain credit of time. You have used more than that, and that's it for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's leave it at this, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one thing. If I may be allowed, every time you're timing me 30-second fractions, you don't treat the Prosecutor like that. I'm being stop-watched every time here. What are they controlling and what is the territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, on the substance, the witness has already answered and we'll surely have the opportunity to come back to this during cross-examination. I really have this in mind, and if there are further doubts, we shall come back to this. My colleague said it's over, so the Bench says it's over. Witness, I have a technical question for you which is not a substance question. Can you confirm that you authored a report which, in your version, has 271 paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can you confirm that there are footnotes in your report, and in the B/C/S version there are 158 footnotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I shall ask the Registrar to display page 82 in B/C/S, 4D28-1062, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat the page of the report. It's page 82 in the B/C/S version, and the number is 4D28-1062.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my mistake. I should have said at the end that the number for this report in e-court would be 4D1731. The document would be tendered under that number. I do apologise for this omission on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic, but I want page 82 in B/C/S. Page 82 is the page I want, page 82 of the report in B/C/S, and that's it. So please don't take the floor. I know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but we have to look for the page, because the Croatian report is in my possession and I carved it up into chapters. One of my colleagues may be able to give me a hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the screen. Registrar, I would like to see the footnotes, so please display the text. This is it. Witness, take a look at this. This is page 82 of your report. There are footnotes, and you quote documents. We're talking about footnotes 133, 134, 135, 136, and 137. I can see that the footnotes are in English. Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I am fully familiar or relatively familiar with military terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are documents you quote in your footnotes, you quote, so P44747 [as interpreted] and so on and so forth. Have you read all these documents before inserting them or using them in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for everyone to understand well, as regards footnote 133 -- I'm going to take a footnote which is visible to avoid any problem. Let's take 134, which is "4D00780," which is in the first paragraph of page 82. Can I infer that you've read the whole 4D00780 to draw the conclusion which is in the Roman number V in the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is all I had to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I only put a comment on the problem of the transcript we have before it went. This is on the page we just -- we just have on the screen, line 14. There should be a response of the witness, but it said: "No interpretation." It was clear that the witness, to His Honour Judge Antonetti's question, said, Yes, but perhaps the question should be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, you had said, Yes, but this wasn't recorded. My question to you had been whether footnote P4747, if you -- as regards that footnote, if you had read it and if you had used it in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. This "Da" was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have another technical question, Witness. Maybe something has escaped my attention, but could you explain why your original version has, as you have just confirmed, 271 paragraphs, while the English translation that we have before us has 281 paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think they both have 281, actually. I've just been looking. I don't know where the "271" came from, but I think if I may -- we're on technical matters. Both versions we have appear to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perjury, perjury, because the witness really confirmed that it was 271, or perhaps a mistake of the translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- but we will not prosecute this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When a learned Judge puts a page number in those terms, witnesses will often just go along with it, Your Honour. That's part of the problem sometimes on these practical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I don't think we should take this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Questions from the Defence team for the cross-examination, with the understanding that two hours had been granted to the other counsels. So let's start with Mr. Karnavas, whom I would like to greet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I don't believe I will have too many questions. I've been allotted about 40 minutes among our -- my colleagues, but I don't believe I will take the entire 40 minutes. We will be distributing some documents. It is -- I highly doubt that we will even need to go to the documents, sir. But in the event we need to, we will -- they're there. Let me pick up, sir, where we left off with General Praljak's questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm going to wait until the distribution -- perhaps the usher could make two trips, as opposed to one. It might -- my apologies for this delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just going back to your background, I had an opportunity to read your CV, and it would appear that you've attended just about every course offered to an officer in order to reach the highest possible grade in the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in addition to having attended all these courses, you also have some practical experience being a soldier for all of your career, so you also have boots on the ground, as they say, experience?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in addition to that, you've also taught, which means that aside from having that practical experience, you also have the theoretical experience that you were able to provide to students who were trying eventually to be officers like yourself on the field, ready in the eventuality a conflict or a war broke out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to this zone or area of responsibility, and I'm sure -- I'm sure you've heard of these terms. These are not foreign to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday you were directed to I believe it was paragraph 24 of your report. You don't have to look at it. But in connection to the question referencing to paragraph 24, you indicated that it would be a three- to five-kilometre zone or area of responsibility, depth-wise. At least that's what I understood. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then there were some other questions, and there was one particular question, I believe it was from President Antonetti, who asked about brigades and the names of these brigades, because it appears, and I believe you confirmed, that the brigades were connected to the municipalities, hence why they had names that were representative of the municipalities from which they hailed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you know, I'm not -- I've never served in the military, but I have spent quite a bit of time reading JNA documents, for this case and for other cases. And when it comes to the brigade rules now, it would appear that the material that was used by the JNA, material that you used to train, provided schematics so that when somebody was out there in the field, they would know exactly where the depth would be; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now -- and when we look at the rules for the brigades, at least, it would appear that we're talking about 15 to 20 kilometres, although that could change depending on the terrain; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, and correct me if I'm wrong, that that would -- as far as the area or zone of responsibility for a brigade, that would be provided to the brigade commander by the corps commander or his superior, although if one wasn't provided, the brigade commander would be in the position and obligated to designate his own area of responsibility, including the depth behind the confrontation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm not going to go into the schematic, unless the Court wishes to see that, but in that depth you would have, for instance, a designation for the forward command post, where the reserves may be, where certain artillery may be located, and so on and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to -- I want us to go to, say, an urban area, an urban area where there's conflict in this urban area. All right? Are you with me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, let's say, Mostar, for instance, would be a good example. I suspect that you've been to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I suspect, in your involvement in this case, you learned that more or less in the middle of Mostar there's a place -- there's this road referred to as the boulevard, and that was the confrontation line that separated the two forces. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No dilemma there? You need to answer it. So there's no dilemma. Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- when we're talking about this confrontation line, the area of responsibility in Mostar is not simply this boulevard, but it goes further back, and the depth could be 15 or 20 kilometres or even further behind, depending on what is happening on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, when we're talking about the area of responsibility, if you have a tank placed someplace, artillery is placed someplace else, that would be within the confines or within this zone of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as a commander, if you were in charge, if you were responsible, you would be responsible not just what is happening in front of you and beyond, but also what is happening behind you, that depth area that we're talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if soldiers in that depth area are doing something that is contrary to what they should be doing, they need to be investigated and perhaps even punished, if necessary; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was -- there was a pregnant pause there, and so maybe you can help me out, because I also had a chance to look at some other rules dealing with the Law of Wars. You know, as I understand it, JNA officers were responsible to understand the necessary legal instruments, international treaties, conventions, and what have you, that apply to war situations, how to treat civilians, how to treat prisoners of war, and what have you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And a commander would be responsible, as I understand it -- you know, that he would be held accountable if he knew or could have known - those are the terms used in the rules, we here use "would have" - but could have known, okay, they would be responsible to -- if they failed to prevent or then failed to punish; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now that's -- I'm just mentioning that because of that pregnant pause of yours, because I want to make sure that we're in agreement that everything that happens within this zone of responsibility, the commander is responsible for, albeit, you would agree with me, a commander is not omnipotent and omniscient. He can't be everywhere and know everything; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, at this point I would like to object. With regard to the lack of precision in the term "responsibility," I believe that we should have to pin-point responsibility for what. If we're not precise with regard to one aspect of responsibility, one could conclude that a military commander could be responsible for absolutely everything that is happening in an area of responsibility. So I would like you to order my learned friend Karnavas to be more precise when it comes to the term of "responsibility." What activities does he have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, so that there is no ambiguity, could you ask the witness to specify this notion of responsibility which he may understand according to your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President and Your Honours. And as you well know, my practice generally is to go from the general to the specific. We just covered something rather general. Now we'll go to the specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's just say, sir, that a particular soldier commits murder, kills a civilian - it doesn't matter who that civilian is - or robs a civilian, or rapes a civilian. The commander would be responsible, assuming that he is capable, under the circumstances, of knowing of it, to either prevent or punish that event; am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a commander in such a case cannot be held responsible. He can only be responsible if he did not take adequate measures once he had learned about the incident. What does this mean? This means file a criminal report, place such a soldier into custody, and report to either the civilian or military authorities or, rather, refer the matter to them for further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And before the objection that was raised, I indicated that a commander cannot be ever knowing and ever present to know what's going to happen or to prevent everything. So it all depends on the circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's all I wanted to get out of that part. But since we're on that, we know that soldiers would serve some time on the line and then, as you indicated, sometimes they would go home because, at least in this instance, there were no barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so when a soldier is relieved -- is relieved from the front and goes home, be it in the city or be it in some village, and I want you to follow closely the scenario, with the soldier carrying his weapon and having also the ammunition with him, if on his way to home or while at home he or she, if a woman is in the armed forces, commits a crime, if a commander were to learn of that, he would be responsible to take the necessary actions because that individual is still a member of the armed forces, is still a soldier, and the commander is still responsible for that soldier's behaviour; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, a commander most probably will not learn about the act directly, but rather from the civilian authorities, which are already duty-bound to take measures before they even inform the commander and take some steps even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. But you would also agree with me, and I don't want to dwell on this concept too much, that a commander cannot willfully be blind? In other words, a commander cannot take certain actions to make sure that no information comes his way that he would then have to react. You would agree with me that a commander cannot do that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go back to another concept. Well, just one more thing about this area or zone of responsibility because there's been a lot of controversy. You've just confirmed that the brigades -- sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I would like to ask a question to go a bit further on your question. Witness, you told us that according to your expert report, a third of the soldiers were on the front-line, one-third in the reserve, and one-third on leave at home. So I assume there is the situation of those who are back home -- you have a soldier, Mr. X, who is back in his village, in his farm, and who, for some unknown reason, is going to rape his neighbour, and the information comes to the knowledge of the brigade commander. According to you, who is competent? Is it the military prosecutor or is it the civilian prosecutor, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military prosecutor, if there is one available, if there is, indeed, a military court and a military prosecutor's office. In the former armies in the former Yugoslavia, such courts did not exist. In Slovenia, for example, they don't exist even to this very day. The question is, Your Honours, how the commander learned about the incident, about the crime, whether he learned about it directly via his intelligence service or through the civilian intelligence service. In such a case, if soldiers are at home, an incident is first reported to the civilian organs and only then to the military organs. Most probably, such a crime would have already been dealt with by the civilian authorities in cooperation with the military authorities in the respective territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether in this instance, in the situation that you were asked to provide an expert report, whether a military prosecutor was in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have not studied the document in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't want to dwell on this too much, but I think we can go on to the next topic which had to do with control, because this issue -- but before that -- I'm getting old, myself, as one of the Judges indicated about age earlier. I wanted to ask you about zones or areas of responsibilities, because yesterday you limited your to three to five kilometres. That struck me odd. Now we've got it up to 15 to 20, at least with the brigades. But when it comes to the corps, we're talking anywhere, I think it is, around 60 to 100 kilometres, somewhere around there; right? I'm talking textbook now. I'm not talking about what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something to your words, sir. When we are talking about an area of responsibility and the depth of the area of responsibility of a JNA brigade of 15 to 20 kilometres, what is meant is the complete deployment of all units, which means all the battalions, including the reserve battalions and logistics units. They are all in place and ready for combat. As for the combat activities, themselves, they take place on the very front-line which is in depth of the active battalion, which is three to five kilometres. And as far as I know, not a single brigade of the HVO was in the classical deployment for defence, as is required by the rules of the JNA or any other army in the world, which would have been 15 to 20 kilometres. There is one more thing that I would like to correct. In settled areas, in urban areas, that depth is very shallow and does not exceed a couple of kilometres, for example. To be very concrete, the Soviet Army, several divisions were defending Stalingrad along the depth of between 1500 and 1700 metres in settled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a second. Yesterday, you kept talking about three to five kilometres, and granted we're not talking about the JNA, we're not talking about having the JNA working alongside with the Territorial Defence, we're not talking about the way it should have been planned prior to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. I understand that. Now, how many documents have you actually read concerning the various places to actually be able to give an opinion to the Trial Chamber that the zone or the depth should have been anywhere from three to five kilometres? Because that's what you limited yourself to, and the point that I'm trying to make is, when we're talking about brigades, whether they were established properly, whether they were manned completely. Given that many of them had professional JNA officers, they would at least know, and I would have expected you to at least tell the Trial Chamber, that the depth would have been anywhere from 15 to 20 kilometres behind the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if an entire brigade would be lined up for defence, which was not the case in the HVO. That would be a normal situation in any normal operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So yesterday, when you were talking, you were talking theory as opposed to what was really happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're shaking your head. That means a yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have to make my record, so -- now, because -- let's go to the next topic, which is control, because you've indicated -- yesterday, again this issue of control came up, and it was in your testimony, and I believe I have it here on page 31 from yesterday. There was a topic that came up on control, and you talked about it, and then you said at one point, and it's at line 22, "control, in the military sense." Okay? So -- and this is -- I guess I want to talk about a place like Mostar. When you say "control, in the military sense," you more or less indicated that Mostar is the zone of responsibility of the commander of Mostar, right, or did I get that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now -- and then you've indicated that if somebody commits a crime, they would -- you would expect the civilian police to act first, maybe inform the commander or have it go up the line. Now, did you actually see anything -- any documents, and if so, if you could give us a ballpark figure of how many, as to what exactly was happening in Mostar, concretely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about that. I've not had such documents. As you have seen, most of the documents are of a formal and legal nature. There were orders and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would be fair -- I mean, to be fair to you, because I don't want you to think that I'm being unfair to you, you looked at the documents, ones that were provided to you or that you searched for, that you thought were necessary for the limited purposes for which you were asked -- you were asked to render an opinion; correct? Based on your remit, you acted accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to share with you one document, because I want to go back and kind of link it up with the civilian aspect that you've indicated, and perhaps you might be able to assist us. And the document is 1D02006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's two or three pages -- two pages, Your Honours. I believe everybody has a hard copy. The witness may need some help, Mr. Usher. We'll provide that to you. 1D02006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have a hard copy, sir, and it's in a language that you'll be able to follow. It's in the binder -- one of the binders that we gave. Okay. If you could look at that, and I would like everyone to sort of spend a moment looking at it. It's dated 2 September 1993. If we go to the second page, it's signed by Branko Kvesic. He's the head of what would appear to be the Department of Interior, at least from the letterhead, that's what we can glean from. I take it this is a document that you have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go through it, and I'm going to take some time, from the first paragraph it says: "Immediately after fighting broke out against Muslim armed forces in the town of Mostar on 9 May 1993, and at the order of operation" -- "and at the order," I underscore that for everybody, "at the order of the Operation Zone South-Eastern Herzegovina, a certain number of members of the civilian police were engaged on the forward front-line." Now, let me stop right there and ask a question. It would appear from this document that whoever is in command of the operations zone had the capacity at that time, at that place, to issue an order for the civilian police to be mobilised to be at the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one objection. From what my learned friend has just read, it doesn't arise that the commander of the operations zone had the power to issue an order on mobilisation. He could only do that if the civilian police were to be subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to quibble about technique, but this can be done on cross-examination or redirect examination. I am entitled to conduct my cross, albeit as nonsensical as it may be to my colleague. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from this an order is issued, an order of the Operational Zone South-Eastern Herzegovina. I'm asking you: Do you know -- and you can say yes or no. Do you know concretely whether the commander of the operational zone or somebody within the operational zone had the capacity, had the ability, had the right, had the power, to issue an order for the civilian police to be at the line? Yes, No, Maybe, I don't know, those are the universal choices.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move on. We'll skip a number of paragraphs. We talk -- and then we go a couple of paragraphs. It says: "On 10 June 1993, we issued an order," "we issued an order to set up two police companies, the first company consisting of members of Mostar Police Station and the 2nd Company consisting of members of the police stations in Capljina, Citluk, Ljubuski, Grude, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Neum, Ravno." We can skip a paragraph, and then it says: "The 1st Police Company, with a total of 120 members of the Mostar Police Station, also joined by 60 members who had already been in combat for a month, took over the forward frontier at the location Ricina Street, the Hit building, the glass building and Mali Park." We go on: "The 2nd Police Company was mobilised on 30 June 1993, was engaged in active combat at several sections of the front ..." And it goes on. We'll move on to the next paragraph: "In addition to a complete company, the Mostar Police Station has engaged another 56 members at the following three locations ..." And it lists them: "And then 18 members since 10 July 1993." Then it goes on: "The Special Police Unit of the Mostar MUP Police Administration, currently consisting of 23 members, was placed at Hotel Ero on 9 May 1993 and is holding the front-line in carrying out other combat tasks at that location." We'll skip one paragraph and then we'll start in sort of the middle of the next paragraph, where it says: "Bearing in mind that some of our units have been engaged since fighting broke out in the town of Mostar and we do not have our own forces or the capability to resolve this problem ourselves, it is understandable that the problem of relieving units must be organised in a different way and a long-term solution must be found. We would suggest that you ask for a detailed report from the command of the defence of the town of Mostar in connection with these problems to determine the number of troops and units needed at the forward defence line in the town and determine a rotation schedule." We'll move on a little bit. It says: "The whole situation is made more difficult by the fact that over 200 policemen are providing physical security to facilities in the town of Mostar alone, about which we have already informed you in our document number," and it lists the number, "on 19 August 1993. It is well known that public law and order, and the crime situation in our area, is very complex. Mysterious murders are taking place, private property is being stolen, the curfew is not respected. Public law and order are being violated, and the civilian police are in charge of all this. These problems were discussed at the HZ-HB government session, and it was decided that these trends must be energetically curtailed. With this report, we only want to draw your attention to the fact that so many of our policemen are currently engaged in other tasks and we do not have any strength to undertake any serious tasks in the sphere of security." Then it goes on: "At the order --" "at the order of the HVO Main Staff," and it lists the number, "on 7 August 1993, we also set up the 3rd Police Company made up of our employees from the area of Livno PU, Travnik PU and Derventa PU. The company is engaged in the Blidinje area, where it's carrying out all the tasks ordered. The duration for which this unit will be engaged is not given in the order of the HVO Main Staff." Now, Colonel, having shared this document with you, it would appear at least from the document - I wasn't there, you weren't there - but at least from the document it would appear that the military is commandeering or is taking away from the civilian authorities valuable resources such as the civilian police. You know, I'm sure there was a good reason, but nonetheless they were taking them and putting them on the front-line or placing them in areas for military purposes as opposed to civilian purposes. Would you not agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Despite everything, my answer needs to be reasoned. I've been looking at this document. There were 200 policemen securing the facility. That is also a police task, a civilian police task, to secure facilities. The 3rd Company was in the Blidinje area. As far as I know, the HVO were not there. They would have to secure the road through Blidinje. The fact remains the military police cannot be subordinated to the army in normal circumstances, whereas here I think there is a document missing based on which the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which is in charge of the police, gives a task to the police. The military commander, himself, had no right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm told there's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you're saying that the fact remains that the civilian police cannot be subordinated to the army. That's what you're saying; right? That's what you said? I just want to make sure that the transcript is correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you said "in normal circumstances." Would it be fair to say, sir, since you haven't looked at the documents, you weren't even asked to look at them, you haven't spent much time over there, you're not in the best position at this point in time to tell us whether these were normal circumstances or not; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether circumstances were normal or extraordinary. I suppose there was a war going on in Mostar, so the circumstances could be defined as extraordinary or exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you cannot sit here with any degree of certainty and say that the military did not order the civilian police to be subordinate to it and to put it in the front-line; you cannot say that, can you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to the answer of my question and I would object at this point to any interruptions. I understand it hurts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't hurt at all. No, Your Honours, it's not about hurting. I just want to draw everyone's attention to the fact that my learned friend, Mr. Karnavas, has put together his examination of Mr. Gorjanc as though Mr. Gorjanc were a factual witness; whereas, in fact, Mr. Gorjanc never studied the situation in Herceg-Bosna, nor indeed did we ever want to call him here as a factual witness. He provided us with his opinions. He's here to give us his opinions. As for the specific situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this can only be done based on documents that we have been showing him, and on that basis alone. Therefore, I don't think we can outright discredit Mr. Gorjanc simply because he doesn't know something about Herceg-Bosna, whereas he was not called to appear here in the first place as a fact witness for Herceg-Bosna. Just to avoid a misunderstanding. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I -- if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, please, just respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can't have it both ways. You can't have him to say, whenever it suits us, he's just here as an expert, and just moments ago he's giving me answers as if he's a fact witness. Look at the previous answer. And that's why I'm going back and saying that since he hasn't studied the situation, hasn't read the documents, hasn't met anybody, hasn't discussed it, he cannot, with any degree of certainty, military or otherwise, tell us whether in that time, at that place, the military was not subordinating and not taking away from the civilian authorities its civilian police to do military tasks. He cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me -- go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one at a time. I mean, somebody -- let's control the courtroom a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think my learned friend Mr. Karnavas should not be meting out advice like that. We've been here for over three and a half years. We know each other full well. The witness never said anything like that. Nowhere in his report does the witness claim that in Herceg-Bosna there was anything that was going on or was not going on. When he addressed subjects that had to do with Herceg-Bosna, he stated in no uncertain terms, and, Your Honours, we played close attention to that in terms of this opinion being provided based on certain documents. Should anyone else come up with documents indicating that there was no communication between Jablanica and Mostar, then the witness can amend his opinion and give us a different one. Another thing that I wish to draw your attention to is for our military expert to be positioned in the same way as the OTP military witness previously, and the witness I mean is Mr. Andrew Pringle. It was clear as day that he was no factual witness, but that he was going to be addressing certain documents from Herceg-Bosna and providing his opinions based on his military background and on military theory. That was the only thing that we expected Mr. Gorjanc to do, and that's the only thing we wanted him to do. Therefore, I would like to have this examination conducted in such a way as to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. And I -- I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to complement my lead counsel. I just raise the question Mr. Karnavas says the witness is giving answers as if he's a fact witness. We'd invite Mr. Karnavas to point precisely to where he gives -- well, his co-counsel says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 69, page 69, line 8 to 16. He said he looked at this and he began -- he looked at the document and he began giving factual answers based on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that makes the point, because he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The point is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Control of the courtroom, Mr. Karnavas, does require you, with respect, for a moment, please, to just let me make my point and then you can make your point. It is my objection at the moment, so if you would just sit down while I make my objection, then I will sit down and you can answer it. That, I think, is the normal, courteous way of dealing with it. I've been looking at this document. There were two -- it's quite obvious the witness is gleaning the information from the document, working on the information from the document, not giving evidence as a factual witness, not saying he was there, not saying he has any first-hand knowledge. He's doing exactly what an expert witness should do. After all, Mr. Karnavas has shown him and read through this document to give him the material in the document on which he expresses his evidence. He is not giving evidence as a factual witness. We don't claim he is, and he hasn't crossed that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to take the floor, I would like to say something, and I'm not talking about the substance, but I would like to say the following: This is Mr. Karnavas' cross-examination. Hence, in his line of questioning he expresses his view and Mr. Prlic's view of -- on the issue of the civilian or military police in Mostar. On the basis of document 1D02006, Mr. Karnavas is asking questions to the expert witness, who is not a fact witness, as we all know. Let us -- let Mr. Karnavas be. Under the procedure, the party who summoned the witness is entitled to ask new questions under redirect, so let's wait for him to have completed his line of questioning to counter-attack, because you're raising objections in front of the witness, who may or may not understand the issue. And if he does, since this is your witness, he'll take your side now. Let me remind you that this is the Court's witness now, so I've always said so. Let the one do the questioning do the questioning, and after that, in your redirect, you take the floor to correct or change slightly what has been said according to the answers. This is a theoretical problem or a theoretical issue on civilian/military police. For four years, we've been dealing with this topic, so we're familiar with it. So it's interesting to know Mr. Prlic and Mr. Prlic's counsel's view on this, and then you can intervene during redirect, because we're wasting time, because what the Judges and everyone else are interested in is to know whether the civilian police and military police can or not be re-subordinated; if not, what are the respective prerogatives of the parties? This is what we're interested in, and we're not talking about a discussion in which we're all bickering about a very simple problem, which boils down to trying to find out what are the competences of the civilian and military police, and perhaps the witness can help us out, possibly. Mr. Karnavas, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by your leave, I would like to say something. I did not study the relationships within the HVO and between the HVO and the authorities, so I can't tell you directly what was the rapport between the military police and the civilian police, and so on and so forth, but I can tell you in principle and answer your question as to whether the military had any legal or any other jurisdiction over the military -- over the civilian police. No, it didn't have, under all military rules. However, if somebody who is superior in the chain of command issues an order to the police, then the military can control it. But let me add to that something else. In the doctrine of All-People's Defence, the armed forces comprised everybody who carried arms, and the police were the best-trained force and they were always the first who joined the army to defend an area. I'm talking about the civilian police. I don't want to talk about this report, because I've not seen it before and I can't be the judge of its regularity and legality. I can't do that. And I would like to thank you for allowing me this opportunity to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Coric's counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say that throughout your presentation, we received a different interpretation in the earphones than what is written in the written translation. You were using the English transcript, and you said that Mr. Karnavas was dealing with the civilian and military police and their relationship. And in the Croatian version we received that it was about the relationship between the military and civilian police, which was not the topic of Mr. Karnavas' cross-examination. I wanted to correct this. And that's why the witness started his first sentence the way he did, because I presume that he heard the same things I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir -- and I want to thank you for that explanation, because that sort of makes my point. When you're discussing the All-People's Defence and you're saying, in principle, what you're talking about is the way that you were -- that you studied and that you taught, how things should be between the military and the civilian authorities in the eventuality a war broke out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one would expect that when Yugoslavia broke up and Slovenia, for instance, became independent, you didn't stop thinking the next day as a Slovenian colonel with Slovenian doctrine; you were still thinking like a JNA officer, although you were now part of the Slovenian armed forces. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I must say that I was one of the founders of the Slovenian doctrine. I immediately embarked on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the next day you stopped -- you were no longer -- you had no mindset of the JNA doctrine and now you were following a Slovenian military doctrine; is that what you're trying to tell us, sir? Because what I'm getting to is this, and this is based on what you said yesterday, that it would have been easier, to some extent, for armies to be set up because they had a cadre of officers that were already trained, they were all JNA officers, and I put to you, sir, that once Yugoslavia broke up, they stopped -- they did not stop thinking like JNA officers. They may have improvised, given the situation, but it was the doctrine that you have been lecturing to us for the last day or two; correct? That's the doctrine that they were supposed to be employing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say only that the way we were thinking was in consistence with International Rules of Warfare, not only the doctrine. That doctrine was just one part, and the Rules of Warfare are comprised by that doctrine when the use of the troops is in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just let me conclude here. When you were asked to perform this report of yours, and what we see is basically theory based on JNA and All-People's Defence, you were not asked to look at any documents that might be meaningful for us to understand what exactly was happening on the ground; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when you say that "under normal circumstances," in your previous answer, what you're really telling us is, This is the way things should be because this is how we were taught, and this is de jure, at least, how the military is supposed to function vis-a-vis the civilian authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that these are not normal circumstances. This is a civil war in one of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, where all sorts of things are happening that were not necessarily -- neither side or sides -- all the sides were not necessarily prepared for; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So as you sit here today, you cannot say to us, with any degree of military certainty, as an expert, that is, whether the military on occasion, depending on the circumstances, depending on the place, may have acted beyond its legal authorities and may have de facto taken on authorities or used resources that would have been or should have been under the auspices of the civilian authorities; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as you cannot confirm or just as you did not know, for instance, that there was a military prosecutor operating at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with that, sir, I want to thank you very much for coming here and giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's about time to have a break. Let's have a 20-minute break, and we'll proceed with the other Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's resume the hearing. We had finished with D1. Let's proceed to D2, Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone. The Stojic Defence has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We've already settled the case of D3. D4 now. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We are D5. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, D4 had already intervened, so that's D5. Now D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now the Prosecution's turn. But before that, I would like to ask a question to the witness. But perhaps my colleague will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, it's an entirely technical matter. The answer of Mr. Ibrisimovic has not been recorded in the transcript, and I guess that it is, No questions. Is that correct, Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question. You talked about Stalingrad at a given stage. In your military studies, in the training you attended, in the classes you received or gave, are you familiar with Stalingrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're familiar with it, so you know that in 1942, in Stalingrad, there were three lines of defence. Then around July 17th, 1942 -- why July 17th? Well, it's four days after my birthday. That's how I know the date. So on the July 17th, 1942, there was a fourth line of defence, and Stalingrad was held by the Russians, by the 57th and 58th Soviet Armies. And for that fourth line of defence, they had used 160.000 civilians who had been used to strengthen the defence before the German Army, commanded by Paulus, attacked these two Soviet armies. Now, let's come back to the case at hand. We've learned that sometimes the lines were strengthened by having people put at work to dig trenches or just work within the defence lines. Now, according to what you have learned, is it possible to use civilians, as the Soviets did in Stalingrad, to strengthen the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to views that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia, this was something that was done by so-called work obligation units. These were temporary units set up to perform such tasks. Nevertheless, it was never envisaged for them to be used during actual combat operations. As far as I know, at Stalingrad this was used, at least in part, during actual combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you say that civilians can be used for non-combat activities. Okay, I take note of what you say. But if you have a front-line in which nothing is happening, with the occasional firing without anyone knowing where they come from, according to you, in military terms, is it a combat zone by which the use of civilians is prohibited; or is it so that if the area is quiet, the defence can be strengthened by using non-military staff to dig or remove rubble, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of principle, this should not be done, not along the front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you are saying is that for the first line, it's not allowed. But for the lines which are more in the back, is it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further back, yes, unless the lines are not taken by units or the units are to come later, then the civilian workforce may as well jump in, as well as the civilian machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would only like to say that, for the record, that during the Second World War, the Soviet Union was not a party to some of the Geneva Conventions, number 1. And, number 2, that the 4th Geneva Convention on the civilian population was not yet adopted. It was, of course, as we all know, adopted in 1949. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we have a very serious mistake in the transcript, line 23. We still have that on our screens. The response to your question was: [In English] "Further back, yes, unless the lines are not taken by units or the units are to come later ...," et cetera. [Interpretation] The witness didn't say "further back, yes, unless ...," he said "specially," so it should have been further back "yes, especially the lines." [In English] " ... yes, especially the lines, the lines -- if the lines are not taken by units...," et cetera. [Interpretation] It's entirely different, the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Witness, you have received training and you lecture currently. Now, in this context, I would like to ask you the question: As regards prisoners of war, according to you, according to how you were taught, according to the textbooks and the instruments which were in force at the time in Yugoslavia, or even in Slovenia, for that matter, is it allowed to use a prisoner of war for the purposes of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] POWs who are mere soldiers can be used to perform labour, but not along the front-line. Captured officers must never be used for these purposes, except, of course, if they happen to volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that prisoners of war who are private soldiers can be used to perform labour, but not along the front-line; but captured officers must never be used, except if they volunteer. Can we infer from what you say, Mr. Expert Witness, that the use of war prisoners is possible under the condition that they're not on the front-line and that -- not exposed to a threat? Is this what you are saying to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this taught in military academies in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it still taught currently, presently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say. I have been away from the teaching within the army for about ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] Is it working now? It's working now, so let me repeat the question. I want to find out about what was taught in military academies in Yugoslavia on some topics, such as the use of prisoners of war, and let me finish the question. Earlier on, this question was asked by Mr. Karnavas, and this came up several times. According to your training, you should have had a very high rank within the Yugoslav Army, even end up as a general had all these events not taken place; is this true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand you rightly, you had the best possible military training in a country which was not in the Warsaw Pact and which, according to certain military experts, was maybe the second armed force in the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, for a while it was ranked as fourth in Europe, in terms of the number of military conscripts actually in the units, not in terms of the actual fire-power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer has now been written in the transcript. Madam Prosecutor, I will also greet you and give you the floor for the beginning of your cross-examination. The Court has given six hours to the Prosecution for its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gorjanc. Before we get into the substance of your report, the first thing I want to be clear about is the method by which you wrote the report. Do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of your report, you wrote that you were told that you were not expected to produce an expert report of a factual nature, but that an expert opinion would be requested about certain events, "on the assumption that information contained in documents that would be shown to me is correct." Sir, so my question is: In your report, did you note, in the body of your report, the documents that were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the reason I ask is, if you look from about page 1 to about page 25, and this is the part of your report in which you talk about a wartime army, in that part of the report I only saw about three footnotes. Is that because you only referred to three sources?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, I refer to my background and my long experience of training and in military schools. I'm not so much talking about specific documents. This is a general chapter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we should understand that any place in this report where it is un-cited, where there is no footnote, the source of that knowledge is coming from your experience and your training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that any of the documents upon which you based your report, then, are all footnoted in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. Now, much of the questions that I will ask you over the course of all of tomorrow, at least, will rely on the same technique, in that I'm going to show you a document, I want you to assume it to be true, because it will be very likely you've never seen the document before. I want you to assume it to be true, and then I will follow up with a question about it. But before we get there, I'm going to ask you some questions of a general nature. Now, I understand during the course of these events, at least in 1991, you had joined the Slovenian military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless, from 1991 to 1995, you were aware of generally the events going on in the former Yugoslavia, in places other than Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was following that for personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, for example, were you familiar with the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the European community as an independent state in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you also aware that it was admitted as a member state to the United Nations in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the fact that in November of 1991, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna declared its existence? And I'm going to quote here: "... as a separate political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, further, a little bit less than a year later, in August of 1993, that the entity then declared itself to be the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that neither the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna nor the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was ever recognised by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the international community as a state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you also agree that beginning in April of 1992, that the army -- the ABiH, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no more. The Serbs had their own army, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll move on to that. I'm going to ask you to look at your second binder. You have two binders in front of you. One is bigger than the other. The first one is the very big one. The second one is the smaller one. You have it. That's the correct binder. There you go, and you can open that up. And if you can look to P09276, which I believe is the very first document in front of you. It's a map. Okay. Sir, would you agree with me that in December 1990, following the elections, that the area that you see in that map, the area that is outlined in red and has been labelled "Bosnia-Herzegovina," every bit of that area in red belonged to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now if you just go forward about a year to December of 1991, that area, that area in red, remained exactly the same; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then if you go forward a little bit more to May of 1992, and this would be after Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent state and also a member state of the United Nations, that red line that you see was the internationally-recognised border of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. And then at least until -- from that time at least until the middle of 1994, that area within the red part remained the sovereign territory of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, similarly, at the time that it became a member state and internationally recognised, at that same time would you agree with me that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was based at least primarily in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like you now to look at P00476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I would like to keep the map for a while to ask another question. Witness, you have now the map in front of you, and I see on this map that there is your country, Slovenia, and I see that between Bosnia and Slovenia there is Croatia, with Zagreb. During the 1990s, the students -- the Slovenian students who were close to the border, were they studying in Zagreb or were they studying in Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part in Ljubljana, but there were some who studied in Zagreb as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Those who were living close to the border, and I'm speaking about the former Yugoslavia in the years 1990, what was the general, natural trend, to study in a major city like Zagreb, for instance, or to study, because of republican criterion, being in the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, would you stay in Slovenia, or was this question never asked and there was no problem and one was studying in Belgrade or Sarajevo? Was there a ethnical aspect or did students go wherever it was interesting to pursue such studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, the students were studying in Ljubljana because of the language barrier that existed between Slovenia and Croatia. All of them would have completed their secondary education in Slovenia in the Slovene language. One would study in Zagreb or Belgrade, not so much in Sarajevo, not as far as I know, at those universities that didn't exist in Slovenia for certain types of profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. The reason I'm asking this question, General Praljak told us that the students who are in Mostar were going to study in Croatia, and that it was more natural to go and study in Croatia than in Sarajevo, so I was trying to check what he told us by your Slovenian example. So if I understand you rightly, you are telling me that the linguistic factor was important, and due to the fact that some people used the Slovenian language, they might have had more difficulties to go elsewhere; this is the reason why they went to study at Ljubljana. This is what I'm supposed to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Well, thank you very much for these precisions. It was a question which could have escaped many, and I explained why I asked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you could go to the other binder, the bigger one, and we'll go to P00476. It's the third document. This is a document -- I think you had that there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably made a mistake, Madam Prosecutor. Yes, it is in the first binder, the third document of the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So if everyone has that, that's P00476, and this is a document from the same period of time. It's September of 1992, and it's a decision from the Constitutional Court of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in this document, they analyse an event upon which you've already commented, which is the establishment of the Community of Herceg-Bosna in November of 1991, and if you can see, that's number 1. And they also review, if you look at number 5, the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, among some other documents. Now, at the very last page of this document, the Court comes to an opinion, and the opinion is that the challenged documents do not comply with the constitution and law. Now, Mr. Gorjanc, would it be -- would it follow that here the Constitutional Court declared Herceg-Bosna and its army to be illegal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It arises from the document that that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to state an objection for the record. The fact that the Decree on Armed Forces was annulled does not provide a basis for -- the basis for a conclusion that the HVO army was supposed to be abolished as a result of that. I hope my learned friend will take that objection into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... so you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that when it came to the military doctrine at the time, it was the doctrine of the All-People's Defence which was foremost in the mindset of the warring parties in the Croat-Muslim war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed, that's the conclusion you come to in that section of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on paragraph 40 of your report - you don't have to turn there, you can just tell me if this is right - you wrote: "In order to gain a more complete understanding of war events in the former Yugoslavia, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is necessary to be familiar with the laws and other regulations --" or, rather, "the practice of the armed forces of the SFR of Yugoslavia upon which they were based."

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so for our purposes, you would agree that for much of their own doctrine and practice - you know, we'll apply it here to these facts - the HVO and the ABiH, in your opinion, based much of their own practice on SFRY doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, for example, in paragraph 64 of your report - this is the part of your report where you talk about the application of the All-People's Defence - you actually cite the BH Constitution and note that part of the BH Constitution was actually taken from the SFRY Constitution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your report you make several notations to the ABiH execution of SFRY doctrine, whether it be All-People's Defence or other doctrine, so is it your opinion, then, to be clear, that the HVO also adopted the SFRY doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So are there some areas where the HVO did not adopt the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are, there are some.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, specifically, we're talking about military doctrine. Can you tell us, in a general way, what those areas are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did not study the doctrine of the HVO in such great detail, so it's very difficult for me to say, as I sit here. However, what I know, in general terms and from some documents, the relationships within the HVO were not completely in compliance or, rather, were not fully adopted from the Yugoslav doctrine, especially when it comes to the relationship between the Supreme Command, the Ministry of Defence, and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that the HVO adopted the doctrine of complying with the International War Laws or in the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at P05496. I think it's in the binder you're looking at right now, P05496. There you go. This is an HVO document. It's the "Official Gazette" of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and it's the declaration on the adoption of documents on the protection and exercise of human freedoms and rights. And specifically, sir, I'm going to direct you to number 3, where it lists the Geneva Conventions I through IV and the 1977 Additional Protocols. Mr. Gorjanc, this does not surprise you, does it, that the HVO adopted those rules of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second binder, 1D02447. It's 1D02447. Thank you. I'd like to look at this document. This is dated May 22nd, 1992, and this was an agreement that was signed by some parties. It was at the invitation of the Red Cross, and in it the parties came to discuss the application of International Humanitarian Law. If you go through the documents -- if you go to page 2, it talks about general principles, and at the very top it says -- it speaks of the Geneva Conventions. And if we go to the third page, it also talks about, under 2.3, a civilian population and the convention that would be applied there. If you go to the next page, 2.4 talks about the third Geneva Conventions and so on. But the last page shows the signatures of several of the parties who were there, one of whom represented the Croatian Democratic Community. Would you agree with me, sir, that this would be an example of what we spoke about earlier, which is that you're not surprised that the parties adopted conventions regarding International Warfare Law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
